audioScript:
Good morning, Midya. It's Wednesday, June twenty-fourth. Two big structural shifts are breaking today — one in international student policy that will reshape Canadian higher ed for years, and one in AI markets that is worth watching closely as you build your consulting practice.

Let's start with the story that has the most direct implications for your work, because it is genuinely significant. The United States has formally approved fixed-term visas for international students, capping stays at four years. Let that land for a second. The Peterson Institute for International Economics published a clear-eyed analysis alongside this news, warning that the US is driving away international students at a long-term economic cost to itself. And they're right — but the downstream effect for Canada is actually an opportunity.

Here's why this matters so much to you specifically. Every international student or family that now looks at a US university and sees a four-year hard stop on their visa — no pathway to stay, study further, or transition to work — is a student who will compare that against Canada's more flexible study permit and post-graduation work permit system. Canadian institutions that are actively recruiting globally are about to have a stronger pitch than they've had in years. And that pitch requires sophisticated marketing. Brand positioning. Digital strategy. Enrolment marketing built around certainty and belonging. That is your exact wheelhouse.

Layered on top of this, Canada's Federal-Provincial-Territorial Immigration Ministers met yesterday to advance the 2027 to 2029 Immigration Levels Plan. They discussed returning immigration to sustainable levels — which is the careful government language for saying the cap era continues — while also addressing labour shortages and regional needs. The Provincial Nominee Programs were on the table. What this means practically is that the intake numbers for international students over the next three years are being negotiated right now, at the ministerial level, across provinces. BC's priorities will matter here. Any Canadian university you are in conversation with is navigating this uncertainty in real time, and a consultant who can help them communicate clearly to prospective students in this volatile policy environment is extraordinarily valuable.

And then there's a third piece: two Canadian universities have broken into the global top ten on a prestigious ranking — the Daily Hive story doesn't name them, but the signal is clear. When an institution achieves that kind of recognition, the internal conversation immediately turns to leverage. How do we recruit off this? How do we communicate it to donors, to government, to prospective students globally? That is a consulting engagement waiting to happen. If you have contacts at U of T or UBC — the two most likely candidates — now is the time to reach out with a congratulatory note and a question about how they're planning to use the momentum.

Also worth flagging: University of Toronto's faculty association and two other groups are publicly urging Ottawa to act on study permits for Gazan students. This is an ongoing humanitarian and political issue inside Canadian higher ed that is affecting how institutions think about their international brand and their relationships with government. It's not a direct business story, but it's context you need if you're walking into rooms at Canadian universities.

Now let's talk about AI, because today's news is actually more nuanced and strategically useful than the usual hype cycle.

Chip stocks are slumping from recent record highs. Axios is calling it a reality-check moment in the AI buildout, and the key tension they're highlighting is this: the cost of some compute is coming down as cloud providers compete, but the cost of running the actual flagship frontier models — the top-tier systems like the ones you're likely recommending to clients — remains stubbornly high. What that means for your consulting practice is that the budget pressure your clients feel around AI is real and grounded. When a CMO tells you they're worried about the cost of AI-powered personalisation at scale, they're not being conservative for no reason. The economics are genuinely unsettled at the top end.

At the same time, Chamath Palihapitiya was on the Axios Show pushing back hard on the AI jobs apocalypse narrative. His argument is historical: new technology changes what humans do, it doesn't make humans irrelevant. He specifically mentioned that even plumbers aren't being replaced. Now, Palihapitiya has an investor interest in maintaining confidence in the AI sector, so take the framing with a grain of salt — but the underlying point is useful. When you're in rooms with Canadian university leadership or brand teams who are anxious about what AI means for their marketing staff, this is a grounding perspective. The question isn't whether to adopt AI; it's how to redesign roles and workflows around it. That reframe is more productive and more accurate.

On the marketing side, two stories are worth your close attention today.

Unilever's marketing lead, Branden Goodman, gave an interview to Adweek laying out what he calls the new rules of consumer discovery. The core thesis: content creation has to evolve from a campaign mindset to a continuous system. This is not a new idea in digital marketing circles, but when the person responsible for marketing at one of the world's largest consumer goods companies says it publicly and explicitly, it signals that the industry has crossed a threshold. The implications for your consulting work are direct. Canadian universities, for example, are almost entirely locked in campaign thinking — they do a big September push, a spring recruitment campaign, maybe a giving-day effort. The idea of building a continuous content system that serves prospective students, current students, alumni, and donors year-round, powered by AI, is genuinely transformative for them. That's a consulting pitch right there.

Gap Inc. is doing something concrete in this space worth examining. They've announced an AI transformation across their owned marketing channels — Old Navy, Banana Republic, Athleta — built on partnerships with Google Cloud, Zeta Global, and Publicis Sapient. This is an enterprise-scale case study of exactly the kind of AI-in-marketing stack a sophisticated organisation needs. The partnership model is notable: they're not building it in-house from scratch; they're assembling a coalition of best-in-class vendors. That approach is probably the right model for mid-size Canadian organisations too, and it's worth thinking about how you'd advise a client to structure something similar.

And one more signal from the marketing world: news advertising is becoming brand-safe again. GM and The Trade Desk told ADWEEK House that news environments are delivering reach and adjacency that brands had been avoiding for years. If you have clients who pulled out of news inventory during the brand safety panic of the early twenties, it may be time to revisit that conversation. The pendulum is swinging back.

A quick but important note on your BC properties. Canadian mortgage data out today shows that variable rates are now sitting meaningfully below fixed rates — but Canadians are still overwhelmingly choosing fixed. The analysis in Mortgage Professional America Magazine suggests this is pure risk aversion baked in from the rate shock of a few years ago. What it tells you practically is that the market is not responding to rate signals the way economists would predict, which means housing transaction volumes are going to stay somewhat muted even as rates come down. If you're thinking about any refinancing decisions on your Sun Peaks, Langley, or Vancouver holdings, this is context worth having. The variable-versus-fixed question is live, and the conventional wisdom is shifting — but most borrowers haven't caught up yet.

Locally, two things to know before you head into Kamloops this week. First, the Kamloopa Powwow is expecting thirty thousand attendees. That is a major event by any measure — one of the largest Indigenous cultural gatherings in North America — and it will mean significant traffic disruption on key routes in and around the city. Plan your timing accordingly.

Second, Kamloops city council has voted to advance new sheltering limits, citing fire risk and public safety. This is part of the ongoing conversation about how the city manages its unhoused population, and fire risk is the specific trigger here — which matters given BC's wildfire season context. It's a council-level story, but it signals where city priorities are heading.

And the good news from Sun Peaks: Rockin' in the Peaks is back. If you're at the property this weekend, the festival is returning with its mountain-backdrop concert format. Worth knowing.

One global story worth your attention as a senior leader. Trump is bearing down on NATO ahead of Secretary General Mark Rutte's visit to Washington tomorrow. The administration is explicitly conditioning US defence commitments on Europe's willingness to engage on Iran — which is a significant escalation of what has until now been mostly rhetorical pressure. If this results in a material weakening of the trans-Atlantic alliance, the downstream effects for Canada are real: defence spending pressure, trade relationship complexity, and a shifting geopolitical environment that affects how global clients and partners think about North American stability. Not an immediate action item, but worth watching closely over the next 48 hours as the Rutte meeting unfolds.

One health story today from a credible source. STAT News is reporting that an ophthalmology biotech called Ollin Biosciences has raised three hundred and thirty million dollars to move into late-stage clinical trials for eye disease treatments. This is a venture capital and clinical pipeline story rather than a practice-change story, but it signals serious investor and clinical confidence in a new generation of eye disease therapies. If you or anyone in your family is tracking age-related macular degeneration or other serious eye conditions, this is a company and a trial pipeline worth keeping an eye on as data emerges.

That's your Wednesday briefing, Midya. The through-line today is really about positioning — the US is making itself less hospitable to international students just as Canada is recalibrating its own intake policy, and that tension creates a specific, named opportunity for the work you do with Canadian universities. The AI market reality check is actually useful signal for your consulting conversations: it helps you calibrate what's hype and what's real investment when you're advising clients on their AI-in-marketing roadmap. Stay close to the NATO story today — the Rutte meeting could move fast. Have a sharp Wednesday.
